paragraphs.text: A [dark tea](dark:definition) kept since 1983, grown in [Taiwan](taiwan:on-a-label). The record names only the island, so it says where the leaf grew and nothing more about the mountain or township. That makes it an unusual tea for a place whose trade is built on [oolong](taiwan:known-for), a craft that came across the strait with settlers from [Fujian](taiwan:history). Here the leaf was heated and rolled, then left to change slowly in warmth and moisture, where microbes and the leaf's own chemistry darken and mellow it.

At forty-three years, it has had a long time to change. [Dark tea is made to be kept](dark:ageing), and storage decides how fast it changes as much as the years do. The trade does not agree on one way: some keep it cool and dry for a slow, clean change, and others keep it warmer and more humid for a faster, deeper one.

brewing.text: Dark tea takes boiling water. Its leaf is mature and dense, so it gives up its flavour slowly and is hard to overbrew. Rinse it first with boiling water and pour that off within seconds: the rinse wakes the leaf and washes off dust and any stale smell from storage, and an old tea may take a second rinse. In a small pot use plenty of leaf, about 7 grams to 120 ml, then steep very briefly at first and a little longer each time; a good dark tea gives many cups.

notice.text: A smooth, mellow cup with low bitterness and a deep red colour, often sweet and woody or earthy, sometimes with herbal or medicinal notes. A young dark tea can still smell of the pile or of storage; an aged one is usually redder, sweeter and thicker.
